title: What FTIR sees (and what it does not)
key_message: Infrared light makes bonds vibrate: every substance has its own fingerprint, but a component below about 5 % may not show up.
body: We put a little powder on a small diamond and shine [[mid-infrared|infrared]] light on it, invisible to our eyes. The bonds between atoms vibrate and absorb only certain «colours» of this light. The spectrum is the picture of which colours were absorbed: every substance has its own.

But FTIR only sees well what is present in quantity: below about 5-10 % a component may not show up, and substances that are active at tiny doses may be missed altogether. The spectrum is a clue that the expert person weighs; it is not a diagnosis.
for_chemists: The spectrum in the figure is in [[absorbance|absorbance]] (A = −log₁₀T), measured by diamond ATR with one reflection at 4 cm⁻¹ resolution. The [[mid-infrared|mid-infrared]] runs from 4000 to 400 cm⁻¹, about 48–4.8 kJ/mol: enough to make bonds vibrate, not to break them.

The x axis decreases from left to right, as is usual in IR. Above about 1500 cm⁻¹ lies the [[functional-group-region|functional group region]], below it the [[fingerprint-region|fingerprint region]]; some sources place the fingerprint between 1300 and 650 cm⁻¹, so the convention should always be stated.
The detection limit depends on the component, on the contact with the crystal and on the strength of its bands: as an order of magnitude 5-10 %. Very potent substances present in traces are not seen.

figure.alt: Demonstration absorbance spectrum of a powder identified by the service as cocaine hydrochloride, from 4000 to 500 cm⁻¹ with values decreasing to the right. Three bands are marked: a broad band around 2540, the C=O around 1712 and the aromatic C–H around 729 cm⁻¹.
figure.caption: Demonstration spectrum (measured, diamond ATR): three recognisable bands. The identity is a proposal of the service, not confirmed with other techniques.

limit_note.title: What FTIR does not see
limit_note.text: Components below about 5-10 %; potent substances at tiny doses (such as fentanyls and nitazenes); the amount of a substance, because the spectrum tells what is there, not how much. This is why other tests are used too and, when needed, a laboratory.
